opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think what's interesting is the shift in how people think about the interface between humans and models. For a long time, the default paradigm has been turn-based: you write a prompt, the model thinks, gives you an answer, and you go back and forth. That's a bit artificial. Real collaboration between people isn't like that. When two researchers work together at a whiteboard, they interrupt each other, they correct course halfway through a sentence, and they build on partial ideas. An interactive model points in that direction: the model and the human are in a continuous loop rather than taking turns.

From a research perspective, that raises a lot of fundamental questions. How do you train a model when the "episode" isn't a clean prompt-and-response pair, but a stream where the human can step in at any point? What's the right objective? How does the model decide when to keep going on its own and when to stop and ask? That's closely related to things I care about, like how reasoning actually emerges, and how a model represents uncertainty about what the user really wants.

I also think it's a healthy reaction to the trend of making models fully autonomous: just give it a task, let it run for hours, and come back to the result. Autonomy is powerful, but in many real settings the human has knowledge, taste, or constraints that are very hard to put into a prompt upfront. If the model can absorb that feedback naturally and cheaply, mid-process, the whole system can be much more efficient than either the human or the model alone.

So for me the interesting part isn't any single benchmark number. It's the bet that the next big gain comes not only from making the model smarter in isolation, but from redesigning how humans and models think together. Whether that bet pays off depends a lot on execution, latency, and whether people actually change how they work. But I think it's the right kind of question to be asking.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the usual turn-based prompt-and-answer exchange with an interactive model where the human and model work in a continuous loop.

fable-5.1.text:
What I find interesting is that they're taking a very different view of what a model is. Most of the industry right now is in this race where you train a huge model, you put it behind an API, and the user sends a prompt and gets a response. It's basically a batch process. The interaction is one shot, or at most a chat window with a long context.

What Thinking Machines is doing, as I understand it, is treating the interaction itself as the core object. The model is something you work with continuously, you steer it, you correct it, and it adapts to how you work rather than you adapting to its interface. I think that's actually the right framing. If you look at how people really use these systems, the value doesn't come from the single best answer. It comes from the loop, from going back and forth and converging on something together.

From a research perspective, that raises hard questions that I personally find exciting. How does the model learn from a few interactions with a specific person without forgetting everything else? How do you make the model's internal state legible enough that the user can actually intervene? And how do you do fine tuning or adaptation cheaply, on the fly, instead of running a giant RL job every time? Their work on things like Tinker, which makes fine tuning much more accessible, points in that direction. It's an infrastructure bet as much as a modeling bet.

I also like that they're being fairly open about the methodology, the blog posts on determinism in inference, on LoRA, and so on. That matters because if you believe interaction is the product, then the details of how the model behaves under small updates become the whole game, and the community needs to be able to study that.

So the thing I'd watch is whether they can show that a model which is constantly interacting and adapting actually gets better in a way that compounds, instead of just drifting. If they can demonstrate that, it changes how everyone thinks about the lifecycle of a model.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts one-shot or chat-based interaction with working continuously with the model, steering and correcting it in an ongoing loop.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is the shift from a model that gives you an answer to a model that works with you. In a typical interaction today, you write a prompt, the model produces a response, and then you figure out what went wrong and try again. But often you don’t know exactly what you want until you see something concrete.

An interactive model could help with that process. It could ask a useful question, show you a few possibilities, and adapt as you give feedback. The interesting research question is how it decides when to act and when to ask. Asking questions all the time is annoying, but confidently proceeding with the wrong assumption is also costly.

So to me, the exciting part is treating that back-and-forth as part of the intelligence itself. The goal is to help the user reach a good result over the course of an interaction.

r001.rationale: It contrasts one-shot prompt-and-response exchanges with a model that asks, offers possibilities, and adapts to feedback as part of an ongoing interaction.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is the shift from a model that gives you an answer to a model that works with you. Often, you don’t know exactly what you want at the beginning. You try something, see the result, and then refine your goal. So the interaction itself becomes part of solving the problem.

That also changes what we should expect from the model. It needs to recognize when to ask a question, when to act, and how to incorporate your feedback. A very capable model can still be frustrating if it makes the wrong assumption and goes too far in that direction. For me, the interesting question is how to make that back-and-forth productive—how the human and the model can arrive at something better together.

r001.rationale: It contrasts simply receiving an answer with an ongoing process of trying, seeing results, refining goals, and incorporating feedback.
